value: exposure to all seven tested volatiles upregulated the jasmonic acid and salicylic acid signalling pathway
method: healthy potted sweet pepper plants exposed individually to one of seven volatiles ((Z)-3-hexenol, (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, (Z)-3-hexenyl propanoate, (Z)-3-hexenyl butanoate, hexyl butanoate, methyl salicylate, methyl jasmonate) from a polymer dispenser in a closed cage for 48 h; transcripts of marker genes PIN2 (JA) and AMP1 (SA) in young apical leaves against unexposed plants, one-way ANOVA
conditions: cv. Lipari, six fully developed leaves, about 20 cm tall; dispenser release 9.6 mg/day in a 60 x 60 x 60 cm cage, 25 C, 14:10 h L:D; 8 plants per volatile and 8 unexposed plants in a separate chamber (n = 8); PIN2 F(7,48) = 17.19 and AMP1 F(7,48) = 9.565, both P < 0.0001, and PIN2 highest with (Z)-3-hexenol, hexyl butanoate and methyl salicylate; the abscisic acid marker ASR1 was NOT overexpressed by any volatile (F(7,48) = 1.546, P = 0.1749); in Y-tube tests only (Z)-3-hexenyl propanoate (P = 0.0394) and methyl salicylate (P = 0.0078) repelled Frankliniella occidentalis, no preference for (Z)-3-hexenol, (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, hexyl butanoate or methyl jasmonate, and (Z)-3-hexenyl butanoate was a non-significant trend (P = 0.0508); the reported error d.f. of 48 does not match 8 groups of 8 (56)

source.authors: Riahi C, González-Rodríguez J, Alonso-Valiente M, Urbaneja A, Pérez-Hedo M
source.title: Eliciting Plant Defenses Through Herbivore-Induced Plant Volatiles' Exposure in Sweet Peppers

quote: Here, we show that all the tested volatiles induced plant defenses by upregulating the jasmonic acid and salicylic acid signaling pathway.
note: Full text read on frontiersin.org (html and pdf, two passes); CC BY 4.0 (Crossref and article footer). Crossref gives publication 4 January 2022 with DOI year 2021. Airborne exposure of intact potted plants to single synthetic volatiles from a dispenser, a reception test of the plant (gene expression), not extracts. POWO 316944-2 Capsicum annuum L. 'This species is accepted'; WFO wfo-0001019982 Capsicum annuum, accepted (December 2023 snapshot, list.worldfloraonline.org/wfo-0001019982). Other trait of this species on main is sense_light_nonvisual only.

value: salicylic acid content of seedlings increased and jasmonic acid content did not change after exposure to weed volatiles
method: 7-day-old sweet corn seedlings held 7 days in a plastic tunnel with cut mugwort (Artemisia indica) and goldenrod (Solidago altissima) as volatile source (mixture, about 15 g of each), one leaf per plant sampled for JA and SA by LC-MS/MS and compared with unexposed control seedlings, t-test
conditions: Z. mays var. saccharata cv. Canberra 90EX; tunnel 100 x 60 x 60 cm; JA and SA measured for the mixture only, not for mugwort or goldenrod alone; mixture JA not significantly higher (t = 0.761, d.f. = 21, P = 0.455) and SA higher (t = 2.1943, d.f. = 21, P = 0.0396); 12 repeats stated although d.f. 21 implies about 23 observations; field outcomes of the same paper: damaged leaves fell significantly under all three sources (ANOVA F3,212 = 12.38, P < 0.001) but Asian corn borer numbers in ears fell significantly only under goldenrod, and armyworm larval growth fell only on mixture-exposed plants; field timing is given as mid-May and June 2022 in different sections

source.authors: Sakurai Y, Ishizaki S, Izumi S, Yoshida T, Shiojiri K, Takabayashi J
source.title: The exposure of field-grown maize seedlings to weed volatiles affects their growth and seed quality

quote: This treatment did not affect the amount of jasmonic acid in the seedlings, whereas salicylic acid content increased upon exposure.
note: Full text read on frontiersin.org (html and pdf, two passes); CC BY 4.0 (Crossref and article footer). Receiver is the intact seedling; volatile sources are cut weeds. Distinct from the van Doan 2021 and Waterman 2024 maize lines on main. POWO 426810-1 Zea mays L. 'This species is accepted'; WFO wfo-0000907754 Zea mays, accepted (December 2023 snapshot, list.worldfloraonline.org/wfo-0000907754).

value: receiver plants respond to airborne volatiles of insect-damaged neighbours even without green leaf volatiles
method: three-week-old Col-0 receiver plants carrying a VSP1 promoter-YFP reporter shared a divided Petri dish (porous divider, air exchange, no contact) with Arabidopsis emitters fed on by diamondback moth or oriental armyworm larvae; receiver fluorescence imaged in real time
conditions: Col-0 lacks a functional HYDROPEROXIDE LYASE and makes no detectable green leaf volatiles; receivers showed about 30% of peak fluorescence one hour after infestation, when fewer than 5% of emitter leaves were damaged; fluorescence did not rise with the scent of insects alone (no emitter damage), and neither extra CO2 nor extra humidity induced a clear signal (CO2 gave a slight decrease); Dunnett's test, n = 5 (Fig. 1c), n >= 7 and n >= 8 (Fig. 1h, 1i); the text gives no P values for the receiver comparison; recordings ran up to 20 h at 1 h intervals; stimulus dose not quantified
